common_name: Hidatsa Shield Figure Bean (Native American Heirloom Dry Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger passes and soil has warmed to at least 65°F; grow to full dry-down for shell beans rather than picking green.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil, since beans resent transplanting and rot readily in cold ground. Hidatsa Shield Figure is a Native American heirloom dry bean maintained by the Hidatsa people of the upper Missouri River region, producing plump white beans strikingly marked with a dark maroon shield-shaped figure on one side, a traditional variety preserved and shared through indigenous seed-saving networks. Grown on sturdy bush plants, it is left on the vine until pods dry and rattle before harvest, then shelled for storage as a dry bean valued for its rich, creamy texture in soups and stews. Because it is open-pollinated and true-breeding, seed can be saved season to season, continuing a variety with deep cultural and agricultural history.

common_name: True Red Cranberry Bean (Heirloom Speckled Shell Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger passes and soil has warmed; pole plants need a sturdy trellis. Pick at the shell stage around 65 days or let pods dry fully for storage beans around 90–100 days.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil at the base of a sturdy pole or trellis, since this is a vigorous climbing variety. True Red Cranberry is a New England heirloom dating to the 1700s, producing plump, cream-colored pods streaked in deep red-maroon that shell out to reveal beans mottled in burgundy and cream, cooking up to a rich, nutty flavor and creamy texture prized for baked beans and soups. Pick pods at the shell-bean stage for the best flavor and texture, or leave them to dry fully on the vine for long-term storage as a dry bean. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved season to season to continue the variety.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

common_name: Painted Lady Runner Bean (Bicolor Red-and-White Flowered Runner Bean)

planting.note: Sow around or just after last frost at the base of a tall, sturdy trellis; like other runner beans, Painted Lady prefers cooler summers and drops flowers in intense heat.

directions: Sow seeds 2 inches deep at the base of a robust trellis or obelisk at least 6 feet tall; this vigorous climber needs a sturdy support and will overwhelm light structures. A 19th-century English heirloom, Painted Lady is grown as much for its striking bicolor red-and-white flowers as for its edible pods, the two-toned blossoms making it a favorite for cottage gardens and pollinator plantings as well as the vegetable patch. Hummingbirds and bumblebees visit the flowers heavily, and the tender young pods can be picked at 6–8 inches for fresh eating, while pods left to mature yield large, attractively mottled purple-and-cream dry beans. Pick pods frequently to keep the vigorous vines flowering and producing over a long season.

common_name: Tennis Ball Lettuce (Thomas Jefferson's Monticello Heirloom Butterhead)

planting.note: Direct sow or start indoors in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; sow shallowly, since lettuce needs light to germinate.

directions: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. Tennis Ball is a small, dense, dark-green butterhead lettuce documented in Thomas Jefferson's Monticello garden records from the early 1800s, forming tight, tennis-ball-sized heads with a sweet, buttery, mild flavor and crisp inner leaves. Its small, quick-maturing heads make it well suited to close spacing, containers, and succession planting for a steady supply of tender lettuce through the cool season. Keep soil consistently moist and provide afternoon shade as temperatures rise in late spring to delay bolting.
sources: Monticello Thomas Jefferson Center for Historic Plants

common_name: Marvel of Four Seasons Lettuce (Merveille des Quatre Saisons)

planting.note: Direct sow or start indoors in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop, since this French heirloom is bred for reliable heading across a range of seasons.

directions: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. A classic French heirloom whose name translates to 'Marvel of the Four Seasons,' this butterhead forms attractive heads with bronze-red outer leaves surrounding a pale, blushed-pink, buttery interior, valued for holding quality and reliable heading across spring, summer, and fall plantings better than many single-season lettuce varieties. Its rich color and sweet, tender texture have kept it popular in French market gardens and home plots for well over a century. Keep soil consistently moist and provide afternoon shade in warm weather to delay bolting.

common_name: Amish Deer Tongue Lettuce (Heirloom Pointed-Leaf Loose-Leaf Lettuce)

planting.note: Direct sow or start indoors in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; more heat-tolerant and slower to bolt than many loose-leaf lettuces.

directions: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. Amish Deer Tongue is a longtime Pennsylvania Dutch heirloom named for its distinctive triangular, pointed leaves that resemble a deer's tongue, forming loose, upright rosettes of thick, crisp, richly flavored green leaves. It is notably more heat-tolerant and slower to bolt than many other loose-leaf lettuces, making it a dependable choice for extending the lettuce harvest into warmer weather in Gulf South spring gardens. Harvest outer leaves individually as a cut-and-come-again crop, or cut the whole rosette at the base once it fills out.

common_name: Really Red Deer Tongue Lettuce (Red-Blushed Pointed-Leaf Lettuce)

planting.note: Direct sow or start indoors in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; red pigmentation deepens with cooler temperatures and more sun.

directions: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. A red-leaved selection of the classic Amish Deer Tongue type, Really Red Deer Tongue forms upright rosettes of triangular, pointed leaves flushed deep burgundy-red over green, the red intensifying in cool weather and full sun, adding strong color contrast to salad mixes and garden beds alike. Like its green counterpart, it is notably heat-tolerant and slow to bolt for a loose-leaf lettuce, holding good quality longer into warm weather than most lettuce varieties. Harvest outer leaves individually as a cut-and-come-again crop for a steady, colorful supply.

common_name: Long Island Cheese Squash (Heirloom Flat Wheel-Shaped Winter Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; as a moschata-type squash it resists squash vine borer better than maxima or pepo types, a real advantage in Gulf South gardens.

directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vines plenty of room to run. Long Island Cheese is a 19th-century New York heirloom named for its flattened, ribbed, buff-tan fruit that closely resembles a wheel of cheese, with dense, sweet, deep-orange flesh well suited to pies, soups, and roasting. As a Cucurbita moschata type, it shares that species' strong resistance to squash vine borer, a serious pest of pepo- and maxima-type squash in warm, humid climates. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and resists a fingernail, then cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks to concentrate sweetness and improve storage life, which can extend several months in a cool, dry space.

common_name: Noir des Carmes Cucumber (Heirloom Black-Spined French Cucumber)

planting.note: Direct sow an inch deep in hills or rows after soil has warmed; a fast-maturing, historic French variety well suited to succession planting for continuous harvest.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep in hills or rows after the soil has warmed, and provide a trellis or ample vine room. Documented in French seed catalogs since the mid-1800s, Noir des Carmes produces short, chunky, dark-green fruit that ripens quickly and is covered in distinctive black spines when young, an old-world trait bred out of most modern cucumbers. It is one of the fastest-maturing open-pollinated cucumbers available, ready in under two months from sowing, making it a good choice for short-season succession planting through the summer. Pick fruit small and young for the sweetest, least bitter flavor, and harvest frequently to keep vines productive.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil in hills or rows; needs a long, hot growing season to fully sweeten.

directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in hills 4 feet apart, or in rows 6 feet apart, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Banana Melon is a 19th-century American heirloom named for its distinctive shape — long, cylindrical fruit up to 20 inches that closely resembles an oversized banana — with smooth yellow skin and pale salmon-pink flesh that is sweet and aromatic when fully ripe. As a winter (inodorus) melon type, the fruit has little external fragrance even when ripe, so gardeners should judge readiness by the skin turning fully yellow and the blossom end softening slightly to the touch. Its long, heat-loving growing season makes it well suited to Gulf South summers with a long, warm stretch to fully mature and sweeten.

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes into warm, well-drained soil in full sun. Harvest small and green, at 2–3 inches, for the classic blistered tapas dish — heat varies unpredictably fruit to fruit, part of the traditional appeal.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes into warm, well-drained soil in full sun. A traditional pepper from the Galicia region of Spain, Padrón is grown almost exclusively for the classic tapas dish 'pimientos de Padrón' — small peppers quickly blistered whole in hot olive oil and finished with coarse salt — and is famous for its unpredictable heat, where most fruit stay mild but roughly one in ten packs a surprising, sharp bite, a trait tied to growing conditions and picking size. Harvest fruit small and green, at 2–3 inches, well before they mature to red, since flavor and the traditional use are built around the small, immature stage. The compact, productive plants set fruit heavily over a long season, rewarding frequent picking.
